prompt: In React Native's old (pre-JSI) architecture, what actually crosses the bridge when you call a native module method like UIManager.measure?
choices: A direct memory pointer to the real native view
A serialized JSON-shaped message (module id, method id, args) queued and flushed in batches
Compiled machine code for the native method
The entire native view hierarchy

prompt: What does JSI fundamentally change compared to the old React Native bridge?
choices: It removes the separate UI thread entirely
It lets JavaScript hold a direct reference to a C++ host object and call its methods synchronously, with no serialization or queue
It replaces JavaScript with Dart in React Native apps
It makes all native modules load eagerly at app startup instead of lazily

prompt: Why doesn't Flutter need a bridge the way React Native does for UI updates?
choices: Flutter apps run inside a WebView
Flutter uses JSI internally just like React Native
Flutter renders every pixel itself through its own engine (Skia/Impeller) instead of mapping widgets onto native UIView/View instances, so there is no second native UI tree to keep synchronized
Flutter doesn't support animations

prompt: What is the main practical difference between Skia and Impeller in Flutter's rendering pipeline?
choices: Skia only renders text while Impeller only renders images
Impeller precompiles GPU shaders ahead of time, avoiding the runtime shader-compilation jank Skia can cause the first time an animation plays
Impeller is written in Dart and Skia is written in JavaScript
Skia requires a native module and Impeller does not

prompt: In the React Navigation native-stack navigator used in Tier 2's React Native app, what actually drives the screen push/pop transition and the back-swipe gesture?
choices: A pure JavaScript animation library with no OS involvement
The real platform navigation controller: UINavigationController on iOS, a Fragment-backed stack on Android
Flutter's PageRouteBuilder, reused via a native module
A WebView-based router

prompt: In Flutter's go_router / Navigator, how is an iOS-style swipe-back page transition actually implemented?
choices: By delegating directly to the real UINavigationController, exactly as React Native does
By Flutter's own gesture recognizer driving its own Animation object, painted by Flutter's renderer to resemble the native transition
It cannot be implemented in Flutter at all
Through a platform channel call on every animation frame

prompt: What problem does a Flutter MethodChannel (platform channel) solve?
choices: It replaces Dart's widget tree with native views
It lets Dart code invoke platform-specific native code (Kotlin on Android, Swift on iOS) for capabilities the Flutter engine can't provide on its own, such as reading battery level through the OS
It is required before any widget can be rendered
It compiles Dart source directly into Skia draw commands

prompt: Riverpod's StateNotifierProvider pattern in Flutter is architecturally closest to which approach in a React Native app that needs the same kind of shared, cross-screen state?
choices: A single screen's local useState call
A global store such as Zustand or Redux, where update logic lives outside any one component and components subscribe to just the slice of state they need
Passing the same callback prop down through ten nested components
Storing the value in a CSS custom property
